subject: Business
title: Why Most Startups Fail
description: A fast breakdown of Why Most Startups Fail for builders.

hook.text: Nine out of ten startups fail. But the top reason isn't money, competition, or timing.

buildup.text: CB Insights studied 101 failed startups. The number-one cause: no market need.

discovery.text: Founders fall in love with their solution and skip asking if anyone has the problem.

twist.text: Even well-funded startups die this way. Quibi raised $1.75 billion and shut down in six months.

climax.text: The pattern is always the same: build first, ask later, then discover nobody cares.

punchline.text: Don't build it and hope. Ask first, then build.

quiz.question: What is the #1 reason startups fail according to CB Insights?

details.summary: Approximately 90 percent of startups fail, and the leading causes are building products nobody wants, running out of cash, team dysfunction, and being outcompeted. Post-mortem analyses consistently show that lack of product-market fit is the single most common fatal mistake.
details.whyItMatters: Understanding why startups fail helps founders avoid the most common pitfalls. The leading cause, building something nobody wants, is preventable through customer discovery and validation techniques that most failed startups never properly executed.
takeaways: Roughly 90 percent of startups fail, making failure the default outcome
The top cause is building products that do not solve real market problems
Running out of cash is usually a symptom of poor product-market fit, not the root cause

faq.question: What are the top five reasons startups fail?
faq.answer: No market need for the product at 42 percent. Running out of cash at 29 percent. Wrong team composition at 23 percent. Being outcompeted at 19 percent. Pricing and cost issues at 18 percent. Most failures involve multiple overlapping causes rather than a single fatal flaw.

faq.question: Does having a great team compensate for a weak market?
faq.answer: Marc Andreessen argues that market always wins. A great team in a bad market still fails. A mediocre team in a great market can succeed because market demand pulls the company forward. Ideally you want both, but if forced to choose, pick a great market over a great team.
